bull_thesis: The bull case is that Bausch + Lomb is a genuinely improving eye-health franchise trading at a discount created almost entirely by who owns it, and that the discount closes when that owner finally leaves. Bausch Health held 310,449,643 shares, about 87% of the company, as of 22 July 2026. That leaves a free float of roughly 47 million shares out of 357 million - too small for index funds and most institutions, which caps the multiple regardless of results. Strip the overhang away and you own a business that, in the second quarter of 2026 reported on 29 July, grew revenue about 8% on a constant-currency basis to $1.394 billion (an acceleration from 6% in the first quarter), with all three segments growing and both surgical and pharmaceuticals up double digits. Adjusted gross margin rose 160 basis points to 62.2%; adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) rose 28% to $246 million, a 17.6% margin, up 260 basis points. Management raised full-year guidance for the second time this year, to $5.44-$5.54 billion of revenue and $1.025-$1.075 billion of adjusted EBITDA. Net leverage fell a full turn year-over-year to 4.7 times. At $16.91 the shares carry an enterprise value near $10.8 billion against $4.76 billion of net debt, or roughly 10.3 times guided 2026 adjusted EBITDA - against eye-care and medical-technology peers in the mid-teens. The November 2025 investor day laid out 5-7% constant-currency revenue growth per year through 2028, an adjusted EBITDA margin near 23% in 2028, double-digit adjusted earnings-per-share growth, and net leverage near 3.5 times by the end of 2028. That plan puts 2028 adjusted EBITDA near $1.4 billion. Conditions the bull case needs: the parent actually completes the separation rather than optioning it for another cycle; the launch-driven growth holds at the 5-7% pace; margin expansion continues so the leverage gate is reached; and the eventual share distribution is absorbed without a prolonged supply overhang. Meet those and a clean, deleveraging pure-play at 12 times 2027 adjusted EBITDA is worth roughly $27 a share.
bear_thesis: The bear case is that we are paying a full price for an undated option, and that the option costs us money when it is finally exercised. Bausch Health has been promising this separation since August 2020. It announced a spin-off and did not deliver one; it carved out 35 million shares in a May 2022 initial public offering instead; it ran a full sale process in 2024 and announced in February 2025 that the process was complete and would not result in a transaction. Six years, three routes, and the stake is essentially where it started. The current filings say only that the parent 'continues to evaluate' a distribution, a sale, or a combination, expressly conditioned on 'the achievement of targeted debt leverage ratios and the receipt of any applicable shareholder and other necessary approvals' - with the warning that approvals may not be obtained 'on the terms or timelines anticipated or at all.' On the 29 July 2026 call the parent's chief financial officer declined to name either a structure or a date, and noted that the 2025 refinancing had 'extended the runway' and increased 'flexibility around the timing and the process.' The parent has bought itself the right to wait, and it will use it. Worse, the flow cuts the wrong way first: distributing 310 million shares to Bausch Health's own holders delivers roughly six times the current free float into a shareholder base that bought a leveraged pharmaceutical company, not an eye-health growth stock. The supply clears before the re-rating, so an investor who buys today pays a pre-event price and then absorbs the selling. Meanwhile the balance sheet does not forgive delay: $5,128 million of debt principal against $367 million of cash at a 7.43% blended rate, with roughly $365 million of interest expense guided for 2026 - more than a third of adjusted EBITDA - $1.4 billion of senior secured notes due 2028, free cash flow of only $90 million in the quarter against roughly $285 million of annual capital expenditure, and a trailing-twelve-month net loss of $171 million. Net debt is about 44% of enterprise value, so a 15% cut to estimates takes roughly 27% off the equity. Confirmation of the bear case would be another quarter of 'evaluating' with no structure named, a slip in the 5-7% growth pace, or a distribution announced into a weak tape.
sop_bull: Event-win value of roughly $26.97 per share. Derivation: take 2027 consensus revenue of $5.80 billion at the roughly 20.3% adjusted EBITDA margin implied by the walk toward the 2028 target of about 23%, giving approximately $1.18 billion of 2027 adjusted EBITDA. Apply 12 times enterprise value to EBITDA - a discount to eye-care and medical-technology peers in the mid-teens, held back for leverage and for the company's number-three position behind Alcon and Johnson & Johnson Vision - for an enterprise value near $14.2 billion. Subtract net debt of about $4.4 billion by end-2027 (from $4.76 billion today, after modest free-cash-flow paydown) to get roughly $9.8 billion of equity across about 360 million shares, or $27 per share. Sensitivity: 11 times gives about $22.80; 13 times gives about $30.30. By segment the value is roughly 45% vision care (contact lenses and consumer eye health, the steadiest cash line), 30% surgical (intraocular lenses and equipment, the fastest-growing and highest-multiple piece), and 25% pharmaceuticals (dry-eye and glaucoma, launch-dependent and the most variable). No credit is taken for cost synergies, an acquisition premium, or index-inclusion flow, any of which would sit on top.
sop_bear: Verified downside floor of roughly $11.80 per share, and it is a valuation floor rather than a contractual one - this is the most important qualification in the file. There is no signed merger, so there is no deal-break price; there is no net cash, no tender at a fixed price, no reverse termination fee, and no contingent value right. Nothing pays the holder if the event does not happen. Derivation: at the low end of 2026 guidance ($1.025 billion of adjusted EBITDA), roughly 8.5 times enterprise value to EBITDA implies an enterprise value near $8.7 billion; subtracting $4.76 billion of net debt (debt principal of $5,128 million less $367 million of cash) leaves about $4.2 billion of equity, or $11.80 per share. Nine times gives about $13.10. For context the 52-week range is $13.09 to $18.92, so $11.80 sits below anything printed in the past year and represents a stress case - a growth stumble, a distribution dumped into a weak tape, or a credit repricing - not a tested support level. Leverage makes this floor softer than it looks: with net debt at about 44% of enterprise value, a 15% cut to the earnings estimate removes roughly 27% of the equity value.
sop_breakdown: Probability-weighted across three outcomes rather than a single path. (1) The separation completes and the overhang clears within roughly two years, the shares re-rate toward a peer-discounted 12 times 2027 adjusted EBITDA: $26.97, weighted 30% - the weight is low because the parent has missed this same promise three times in six years and its own leverage gate is dated end-2028. (2) Muddle-through: no event, but the operating plan holds, revenue compounds at 5-7% and margins expand, so the shares drift toward the analyst consensus of $18.54 and a little beyond as earnings grow: $19.00, weighted 50% - the modal outcome, and notably the one that requires nothing from Bausch Health. (3) Stress: a growth stumble, a distribution absorbed badly, or a credit repricing takes the multiple to roughly 8.5 times: $11.80, weighted 20%. The weighted result is $19.95, rounded down to $19.75 for the leverage asymmetry noted above. Underneath, the parts contribute roughly 45% vision care, 30% surgical, and 25% pharmaceuticals of enterprise value, less $4.76 billion of net debt. Sanity check on the implied multiple: $19.75 equates to about 11.4 times 2026 guided adjusted EBITDA, still a clear discount to mid-teens peers - the base case does not require the discount to close, only to narrow.
risk_reward: Poor at today's price on the base case; only acceptable on the event case, and the event has no date. From $16.91: downside to the verified floor of $11.80 is -30.2%. Upside to the base-case fair value of $19.75 is +16.8%, a ratio of 0.56 to 1. Upside to the event-resolved target of $26.97 is +59.5%, a ratio of 1.97 to 1 - but that upside is gated on an undated, non-binding corporate action controlled entirely by a third party. The board's carried ratio of 2.4 to 1 measured the event case only and did not weight the probability that the event does not arrive. The setup improves materially near $13.50: from there, downside to the floor is -12.6% and upside to the base case is +46%, a ratio better than 3.5 to 1. That is the same asset at a price that pays for the waiting.
catalyst_summary: Bausch Health's roughly 87% stake unwinds and the float overhang clears, re-rating the shares toward a peer-discounted $27 from $16.91 - but after six years and three abandoned routes the event still has no date, no structure, and no binding term, and the distribution itself would dump about six free floats of supply before any re-rating.
dated_milestone: There is no dated milestone for the separation itself. The only published date in the file is end-2028, the deadline for the roughly 3.5-times net leverage target that both companies have named as the gating condition (Bausch + Lomb investor day, November 2025; Bausch Health second-quarter filings, July 2026). The nearest observable checkpoints are the third-quarter 2026 results from both companies, expected around late October 2026, and Bausch Health's fourth-quarter and full-year report expected in February 2027 - each of which is an opportunity for the parent to name a structure, and each of which has passed without one for six years running.
forcing_function: Nothing currently forces a re-rating on a known date. The event that would is a formal announcement by Bausch Health of a distribution or sale of its 310,449,643 shares - a board decision, taken at the parent's discretion, in the parent's interest, and gated on its own deleveraging rather than on any calendar. Three second-order triggers could pull that decision forward and are worth monitoring: the parent reaching its leverage target earlier than the end-2028 plan (it cut net debt $434 million in the June quarter, to about $13.7 billion against $20.2 billion of borrowings, so the pace is real); an unsolicited approach for the eye-health asset, which would restart the 2024-25 sale process from a stronger operating base; or an activist at the parent forcing the issue. Note the perverse timing: when the forcing event does arrive it lands as a supply shock first. Roughly 310 million shares would be delivered to holders who bought a leveraged pharmaceutical company, against a current free float near 47 million shares. The re-rating comes after that clears, not with it - so the announcement is more likely to be an entry point than an exit.
consensus_delta: The market is not wrong about this company in the way our thesis needs it to be wrong, and that is the honest finding. Thirteen analysts carry a consensus target of $18.54 against a $16.91 price - about 10% of upside - with a range of $16 to $23 and a rating split of four strong buys, one buy, seven holds and one sell. Citi has been the most constructive, walking its target up through 2026 to $21 and most recently $24 on the strength of the product pipeline. Consensus expects $5.49 billion of revenue and $0.80 of adjusted earnings per share in 2026, rising to $5.80 billion and $1.08 in 2027. Those estimates are broadly consistent with company guidance, so there is no meaningful earnings disagreement to arbitrage. Where we do differ from the street is on the two ends of the distribution rather than the middle. First, the street is under-crediting the operating inflection: revenue growth accelerated from 6% to 8% constant currency between the first and second quarters, adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation grew 28% with margins up 260 basis points, and guidance has now been raised twice - yet seven of thirteen analysts still sit on hold, and the consensus target implies barely more than 11 times 2026 guided adjusted earnings. The value case stands without any corporate action, and that is under-appreciated. Second, and cutting the other way, we think the street's treatment of the overhang is too benign. Sell-side notes generally frame the separation as a free option that can only help. It is not free. When 310 million shares - roughly six times the current free float - are delivered to a shareholder base that bought a leveraged pharmaceutical company, the mechanical selling comes before the multiple expansion. The consensus effectively prices the destination without pricing the journey. Our disagreement with the market is therefore narrow and two-sided: a better business than the holds imply, a worse catalyst than the bulls imply.
valley_of_death: The next three to nine months carry no single cliff, but several grinding pressures that argue against paying up today. Interest expense of roughly $365 million guided for 2026 consumes more than a third of adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation at a 7.43% blended rate, and against capital expenditure guided near $285 million the company generated $90 million of free cash flow in the June quarter - real progress at roughly 46% conversion year-to-date, but a thin cushion. The company remains unprofitable on a reported basis, with a trailing-twelve-month net loss of $171 million and a first-half loss of $85 million, so any disappointment shows up as a widening loss rather than a lower profit. The nearest maturity is $1.4 billion of senior secured notes due 2028, which is not an immediate wall but becomes a live refinancing conversation during 2027 - and would be refinanced into whatever rate environment exists then. The most likely near-term stumble is operational rather than financial: growth of 5-7% depends on new product launches in surgical and pharmaceuticals holding their pace, and premium intraocular lenses are a discretionary, largely cash-pay category that softens quickly when consumer confidence does. The other live risk is the perverse one already noted - a separation announced into this window would knock the price down first. And the shares are not positioned to absorb a shock: at $16.91 they sit above both the 50-day average of $15.93 and the 200-day of $16.34, in the upper half of a $13.09-$18.92 range, and about 43% above the stress floor. There is no washed-out entry price protecting the position.
positioning_washout: This is the mechanic at the heart of the thesis, and it runs in the opposite direction to how the setup is usually described. Today the problem is scarcity, not supply: with the parent holding roughly 87%, the free float is about 47 million shares out of 357 million. That float is too small for major index inclusion and for most institutional mandates, which is a large part of why the multiple sits at roughly 10.3 times adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation against mid-teens peers. Management has been direct that fixing it is out of their hands, describing the majority-share overhang as 'not within our control' and 'a BHC issue.' The eventual cure, however, is itself a shock. If Bausch Health distributes its 310,449,643 shares to its own shareholders, the recipients are holders of a leveraged, litigation-scarred pharmaceutical company - a credit-oriented, value-oriented, often index-driven base with no mandate to hold an eye-health growth equity. History says a large share of that stock is sold in the first weeks. Roughly six free floats of supply would hit a stock that currently trades about 400,000 shares a day. The offsetting force is that a fully floated Bausch + Lomb becomes eligible for index inclusion, and passive demand would eventually absorb the paper - but eventually is the operative word, and the sequence is selling first, sponsorship second. The practical conclusion: the forced-selling event is something to buy into, not something to own into. That single observation is what moves this name from an immediate purchase to a watch.
moderator_conclusion: This is a good business wearing a catalyst costume, and the committee should size it for what it actually is. Take the event apart first, because it is the reason the name reached this funnel. Bausch Health has been promising to separate its eye-health business since August 2020. It announced a spin-off and did not deliver one; it sold 35 million shares in a May 2022 initial public offering instead; it ran a full sale process through 2024 and announced in February 2025 that the process was complete and would not result in a transaction. Six years, three routes, and the stake stands at 310,449,643 shares - about 87% - as of 22 July 2026. The current filings say the parent 'continues to evaluate' a distribution, a sale, or a combination, conditioned on 'the achievement of targeted debt leverage ratios and the receipt of any applicable shareholder and other necessary approvals,' with an express warning that approvals may not arrive 'on the terms or timelines anticipated or at all.' On the 29 July 2026 call the parent's chief financial officer named neither structure nor date, and pointed out that the 2025 refinancing had 'extended the runway' and increased 'flexibility around the timing and the process.' A sponsor that has just bought itself the right to wait is telling you it intends to. This is a soft, non-binding catalyst with no contractual payout - not the hard, dated, defined-risk setup this funnel exists to buy. Now the floor, which is the other half of a defined-risk trade and is equally absent. There is no signed deal, so no break price; no net cash - $367 million against $5,128 million of debt principal; no tender, no fee, no contingent value right. Nothing pays us if the event never comes. The $11.80 our board carries is a valuation stress case at roughly 8.5 times adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, and it sits below the $13.09 bottom of the 52-week range, so it has not been tested in a year. With net debt at about 44% of enterprise value, a 15% earnings cut takes roughly 27% off the equity - the floor is soft in exactly the place a special situation needs it to be hard. Given no date and no floor, the arithmetic decides it. From $16.91, the fall to $11.80 is 30%. The rise to our reconciled base case of $19.75 is 17%, which is 0.56 to 1 - unattractive. The rise to the event-resolved $26.97 is 59%, or 1.97 to 1, but that requires a third party to act on no schedule. The board's 2.4-to-1 measured the event leg alone. And the price offers no compensation for the wait: the shares trade above both their 50-day and 200-day averages, in the upper half of the range, roughly 43% above the stress case. None of which is a criticism of the company. Bausch + Lomb is executing well - second-quarter revenue of $1.394 billion beat consensus and grew about 8% in constant currency, an acceleration from 6%; adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation rose 28% to $246 million with margins up 260 basis points; guidance was raised for the second time this year; net leverage fell a full turn to 4.7 times. At roughly 10.3 times guided 2026 adjusted earnings against mid-teens peers, the value case is real and needs no corporate action at all. That is precisely why the conclusion is to wait rather than to pass. The decisive judgement is on sequence. When the separation is finally announced, about 310 million shares land with holders of a leveraged pharmaceutical company against a free float near 47 million - roughly six floats of supply into a stock trading 400,000 shares a day. The selling comes first and the re-rating second. Buying today means paying a full price for an undated option and then absorbing the flow it releases. So: wait for the wash-out, and name it precisely. The two triggers are a retest of the $13.50 area, the 52-week low zone, where downside to the floor narrows to 13% against 46% of upside - better than 3.5 to 1 on the same asset; or the separation announcement itself and the supply event it releases, which is an entry, not an exit. Absent either, this is a well-run eye-health company at a fair-to-cheap price with an option we are not being paid to hold. Watch it closely - the operating trajectory deserves that - but leave the capital uncommitted until the price pays for the uncertainty.
interrogator_dossier:
# Bausch + Lomb (BLCO) - Forensic Dossier on the Event

Prepared 3 August 2026. All prices and filings verified against public sources dated on or before 31 July 2026.

The question in front of us is not whether Bausch + Lomb is a good eye-health company. It is whether a specific corporate event - the unwinding of Bausch Health's roughly 87% ownership stake - is real, dated, and binding enough to pay us for the risk of owning the shares at $16.91.

The short answer: the event is real, it has been real for six years, and it still has no date.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC - six years of intention, no completion

The separation story begins in August 2020, when Bausch Health announced its intention to spin off its eye-health business into an independent public company. What actually happened was smaller: in May 2022, a Bausch Health subsidiary sold 35 million shares of Bausch + Lomb in an initial public offering. That created a listed stock with a very thin free float and left the parent holding the overwhelming majority of the equity.

From there the story changed shape twice more rather than progressing. Through 2022-2024 the route was a spin-off: the parent said the remaining stake would be distributed to its own shareholders once leverage targets were met, and it was not. In late 2024 the route became a sale - after rumours moved the stock, the Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization required a disclosure and the company confirmed it was exploring a sale of the whole company to a third party. In February 2025 that route closed with nothing: the company announced that after engaging with potential buyers, the process was complete and would not result in a transaction. The shares fell on the news and Bausch Health kept its stake. Through 2026 the language returned to open-ended evaluation, in both companies' quarterly filings and on both management calls of 29 July 2026.

The pattern matters more than any single step. Each time the route has changed, the destination has stayed the same and the arrival time has moved. That is the single most important fact in this file.

## 2. THE EVENT, TESTED - is it dated and binding?

As of the quarter ended 30 June 2026, Bausch Health directly or indirectly held 310,449,643 Bausch + Lomb common shares - approximately 87% of shares outstanding as of 22 July 2026. The parent 'continues to evaluate completing a separation, which could involve a distribution to its shareholders, a sale transaction, or a combination.' Completion is expressly conditioned on 'the achievement of targeted debt leverage ratios and the receipt of any applicable shareholder and other necessary approvals,' with the filing warning that approvals may not be obtained 'on the terms or timelines anticipated or at all.'

Tested against the three things a hard catalyst needs: a date is absent (no timeline in either quarterly filing; neither management team offered one on 29 July 2026); a binding obligation is absent (no agreement, no offer, no contractual payout - a stated intention only); and a named structure is absent (distribution, sale, or combination all still on the table).

On the parent's 29 July 2026 call, the chief financial officer said the company is 'evaluating multiple ways to translate that asset's value into Bausch Health's share price' and added: 'There are obviously a number of considerations to evaluate and to figure out exactly how do we translate the value of B+L into a BHC share price, and we're looking at all and any avenues to do so.' He pointed to the 2025 refinancing as having 'extended the runway' and increased 'flexibility around the timing and the process.' Flexibility around timing is, from our seat, the opposite of a catalyst. Bausch + Lomb's own management has been candid that this is not theirs to solve, describing the majority-share overhang as 'not within our control' and 'a BHC issue.'

One thing genuinely did move. The gating condition - leverage - is closing. Bausch Health cut net debt by $434 million in the June quarter to roughly $13.7 billion against total borrowings of about $20.2 billion. Bausch + Lomb's own net leverage (net debt divided by adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) fell a full turn year-over-year to 4.7 times, against a stated target of about 3.5 times by the end of 2028. So the door is being unlocked. The published target date for reaching that leverage level is end-2028, which is the closest thing to a date this situation has, and it is more than two years out.

## 3. THE SPONSOR'S CREDIBILITY

Bausch Health is the only party who can fire this catalyst, and its record on this specific promise is poor: one announced spin-off not delivered (2020), one partial carve-out delivered instead (2022), one full sale process run and abandoned (2024-25). Three attempts, six years, stake essentially unchanged at 88% then and roughly 87% now - the drift is share-count dilution at the subsidiary, not selling by the parent.

The mitigating evidence is operational rather than transactional. Under chief executive Brent Saunders, Bausch + Lomb is executing well: second-quarter 2026 revenue of $1.394 billion beat the roughly $1.37 billion consensus and grew about 8% on a constant-currency basis (a pick-up from 6% in the first quarter), with all three segments growing and surgical and pharmaceuticals both up double digits. Adjusted gross margin rose 160 basis points to 62.2%; adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation rose 28% to $246 million, a 17.6% margin, up 260 basis points. Full-year 2026 guidance was raised to $5.44-$5.54 billion of revenue and $1.025-$1.075 billion of adjusted earnings. At a November 2025 investor day the company set out targets of 5-7% constant-currency revenue growth per year through 2028, roughly 23% adjusted margin in 2028, double-digit adjusted earnings-per-share growth from 2026 to 2028, and net leverage near 3.5 times by end-2028.

So: high credibility on running the business, low credibility on delivering the transaction. Those are two different scores, and only the second one is the thesis.

## 4. THE DOWNSIDE FLOOR - what actually backstops the price?

This is where the setup is weakest. There is no contractual floor. This is not a merger with a signed agreement, so there is no deal-break price. There is no cash pile - the company holds $367 million of cash against $5,128 million of debt principal, roughly $4.76 billion net, at a 7.43% weighted average interest rate. There is no reverse termination fee, no contingent value right, no tender at a fixed price. Nothing pays us if the event does not happen.

What exists instead is a valuation floor and a price memory. On valuation: at the low end of 2026 guidance ($1.025 billion of adjusted earnings), about 8.5 times enterprise value to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation implies an enterprise value near $8.7 billion; less $4.76 billion of net debt, that is roughly $11.80 per share, while nine times gets you to about $13.10. On price memory: the 52-week range is $13.09 to $18.92, the shares troughed in that low-$13s area, and traded lower still during the spring-2025 risk-off episode.

So the $11.80 figure our board carries is a stress-case valuation, not a backstop - and it sits below the 52-week low, meaning it has not been tested in the past year. Note also the leverage arithmetic: with net debt roughly 44% of enterprise value, a 15% cut to the earnings estimate takes about 27% off the equity. Debt makes the floor softer than it looks, not harder.

## 5. RED FLAGS

The catalyst, if it fires, hurts first. This is the most under-appreciated point in the file. The forced-seller mechanic works in both directions. If the parent distributes 310 million shares to its own shareholders, those shares land with a holder base that bought a leveraged, litigation-scarred pharmaceutical company - not an eye-health growth stock. Roughly six times the current free float would be delivered into unwilling hands. The supply clears before the re-rating, not after. Buying today means paying a pre-event price and then eating the flow.

Beyond that: the company is still unprofitable on a reported basis, with a trailing-twelve-month net loss of $171 million (loss per share of $0.48) and a first-half 2026 net loss of $85 million, improved from $274 million a year earlier - adjusted earnings are the only earnings. Leverage is heavy: net debt of about $4.76 billion at 4.7 times, with $1.4 billion of senior secured notes due 2028 and a $2.795 billion term loan due 2031 at a blended 7.43%, and interest expense guidance of roughly $365 million for 2026 consuming more than a third of adjusted earnings. Free cash flow is thin at $90 million in the second quarter against capital expenditure guided near $285 million for the year; year-to-date conversion of about 46% is real progress but leaves little room for error. And this is a controlled company with no independent path - minority holders cannot force the outcome. The parent decides, on the parent's timetable, in the parent's interest, and the parent's interest is its own $20 billion debt stack, not our entry price.

## 6. GREEN FLAGS

Revenue growth is accelerating (6% to 8% constant currency between the first and second quarters of 2026) with all segments contributing. Margins expanded 260 basis points at the adjusted earnings line and guidance has been raised twice this year. Leverage is down a full turn year-over-year at both the subsidiary and the parent - the exact condition the transaction is gated on. Valuation is genuinely undemanding at roughly 10.3 times enterprise value to 2026 guided adjusted earnings, against eye-care and medical-technology peers in the mid-teens; much of that gap is the overhang itself, which is the point of the trade. And the franchise is real: a recognised brand with about 170 years of history, plus regulatory approvals and surgeon habit in intraocular lenses and contact lenses that make it hard to displace quickly, even as a distant number three behind Alcon and Johnson & Johnson Vision in most categories.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The parent has quietly stopped promising and started optioning. The language moved from 'intends to spin off' (2020) to 'may include monetization of all or a portion' (2026) - that is a widening of the option set, which reads as flexibility to management and as slippage to us. The refinancing that 'extended the runway' removed the very pressure that would have forced the sale; the parent bought itself the right to wait, and it will use it. Meanwhile the subsidiary's investor-day targets run to 2028, and the parent named those targets as 'an important consideration' in choosing among options - which is a polite way of saying the parent would rather sell a company hitting its 2028 plan than one still proving it.

## 8. VERDICT FOR THE DIRECTOR

Classification: the operating business is strengthening; the event is stalled. Treat those separately and do not let the first pay for the second.

The single thing to weigh before sizing: this is a valuation position wearing a catalyst costume. Everything genuinely attractive here - 10.3 times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation on an accelerating franchise, expanding margins, falling leverage - is a value case that would stand on its own. The catalyst adds no date, no binding term, and no protection, and when it eventually fires it will deliver roughly six free floats of supply into the market before it delivers a re-rating. The price is not distressed either: at $16.91 the shares sit above both the 50-day ($15.93) and 200-day ($16.34) averages and in the upper half of the 52-week range, roughly 43% above the notional stress floor. We would be paying a normal price for an undated option and calling it asymmetry.

On the two secondary dimensions: the moat is narrow but real - brand and regulatory approvals in lenses and surgical implants, with switching friction among surgeons - and it is holding rather than eroding, given the margin expansion. No structural force threatens the terminal value; an ageing population is a tailwind for eye health, with only modest reimbursement pressure on the surgical and pharmaceutical lines. Neither dimension is what decides this name.
